gap: No result ChatGPT got states the inverter's no-load (idle) draw for any 3,000 Wh unit, a fixed 8 W to 37 W that runs every hour the AC is on and takes 384 Wh to 1,776 Wh out of a two-day fridge run.
standout_why: Compared against powerstations.reviews/jackery-3000, wattpowerstation's home-backup guide, power-verdict's best-3000wh guide, thesolarlab's big-stations roundup, lightsonlabs, thepowerstationreport and powersized (goodhousekeeping.com could not be fetched). Five of the seven give no idle watts at all, and three of them (powerstations.reviews, lightsonlabs, thepowerstationreport) size runtime with a flat 85% 'inverter losses' factor. thesolarlab's roundup gives idle only for the Anker F3800 Plus (about 40 W) and BLUETTI Apex 300 (about 20 W), neither a 3,000 Wh candidate. ChatGPT's own answer says only that low-load inverter losses 'can shorten those estimates', with no number. None shows that the fixed draw differs 4.6× between the units it recommends.
decides: It confirms the Jackery HomePower 3000 as the pick for fridge-through-an-outage duty: The Solar Lab measured 8 W idle, the lowest of the five. It also changes the budget order. The Pecron F3000LFP at $899 idles at 37 W, which is 1,776 Wh (58% of its 3,072 Wh) over 48 hours. By The Solar Lab's formula it carries a 1,300 Wh/day fridge about 34 hours, against about 44 hours for the BLUETTI Elite 300 (15 W) and about 49 hours for the Jackery. So the Elite 300, not the Pecron, is the honest value row for a fridge plan; the Pecron's $200 saving costs about 10 fridge-hours. Only the Jackery clears two days on this arithmetic. Separately, BLUETTI's page today says Elite 300 orders placed on or after Nov 27 ship from Dec 28 (31 days out, not the Dec 14 in the desk notes), which touches the four-week rule; its Amazon listing was not checked.

findings.label: Mechanism: idle draw is added to the load for every hour the inverter is on
findings.value: Fridge Consumption (Wh) + (Power Station Idle Rate (W) × Run Time in Hours) = Total Required Battery Capacity
findings.source_title: How Long Will a Power Station Run Your Fridge? (The Solar Lab)
findings.note: The Solar Lab's own formula; it says a station 'consumes a small amount of stored battery power when it's switched on' and that idle draw 'can make or break your power station's runtime'. This page was not among ChatGPT's results. The formula does not add conversion loss separately.

findings.label: Household fridge energy use (The Solar Lab's test of three fridges in three homes)
findings.value: about 1,300 Wh per day; 100 to 200 W while the compressor runs
findings.source_title: How Long Will a Power Station Run Your Fridge? (The Solar Lab)
findings.note: 1,300 Wh/day ÷ 24 h = 54.2 W average; two days = 2,600 Wh before any idle draw. This is the load used in the runtime arithmetic below.

findings.label: Idle draw, measured by The Solar Lab
findings.note: Quote: 'an idle consumption of just 8 watts', 'the best we've seen from any large power station to date'. The review does not state the test conditions. Arithmetic: 8 W × 48 h = 384 Wh (12.5% of 3,072 Wh); 3,072 ÷ (54.2 + 8) = about 49 h on a 1,300 Wh/day fridge. The Solar Lab gives the weight as just under 60 lb.

findings.label: Idle draw and efficiency, measured by The Solar Lab
findings.source_title: Bluetti Elite 300 portable power station review (The Solar Lab)
findings.note: Quote: 'We measured the idle rate around 15W, which is almost double what we've seen on some other recent Bluetti power stations.' Test conditions not stated. Arithmetic: 15 W × 48 h = 720 Wh (24% of 3,014.4 Wh); 3,014.4 ÷ (54.2 + 15) = about 44 h on a 1,300 Wh/day fridge.

findings.label: Idle draw, measured by The Solar Lab
findings.source_title: How Long Will a Power Station Run Your Fridge? (The Solar Lab)
findings.note: The Solar Lab's table: 20 W idle, 1,440 Wh over 3 days. Arithmetic: 20 W × 48 h = 960 Wh (31% of 3,072 Wh); 3,072 ÷ (54.2 + 20) = about 41 h on a 1,300 Wh/day fridge.

findings.label: Anker's own standby and fridge claims
findings.value: up to 5 days of AC standby; 'One F3000 can power a 190W fridge for 42 hours'
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX F3000 Portable Power Station (Anker SOLIX US)
findings.note: 3,072 Wh ÷ 120 h = 25.6 W implied AC idle draw from Anker's own claim. Anker gives no test conditions for the standby or fridge figures. Its feature list says '2 days of cooling an 8 cu.ft fridge'; the 190 W fridge in the FAQ has no stated size.

findings.label: Idle draw and efficiency, measured by The Solar Lab
findings.source_title: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Ultra Review (The Solar Lab)
findings.note: Quote: 'if you leave the inverter running while waiting for appliances like refrigerators or sump pumps to cycle on, the unit will consume around 22W of battery power per hour in the background.' Arithmetic: 22 W × 48 h = 1,056 Wh (34% of 3,072 Wh); 3,072 ÷ (54.2 + 22) = about 40 h on a 1,300 Wh/day fridge. The Solar Lab gives the weight as 72 lb.

findings.label: Idle draw and efficiency, measured by The Solar Lab
findings.value: 37 W idle; 83% efficiency at a sustained 3,600 W
findings.note: Method: 'charged the battery to 100% and let it fully drain with only the inverter switched on... we calculated a 37 Watt idle draw.' Arithmetic: 37 W × 48 h = 1,776 Wh (58% of 3,072 Wh); 3,072 ÷ (54.2 + 37) = about 34 h on a 1,300 Wh/day fridge. The Solar Lab gives the weight as 63 lb.

findings.label: What the rival pages use instead: a flat 85% factor
findings.value: runtime = rated capacity × 0.85 ÷ watts; HomePower 3000 runs a 41 W fridge about 63 hours
findings.source_title: Jackery 3000: the 3000 Pro, the HomePower 3000, and which to buy
findings.note: With the idle formula on the same 41 W fridge: Jackery 3,072 ÷ (41 + 8) = about 63 h, so the flat factor happens to fit an 8 W unit. Pecron 3,072 ÷ (41 + 37) = about 39 h, so the flat factor would overstate it by about 24 h. lightsonlabs and thepowerstationreport use the same 85% assumption.

findings.label: Per-outlet limit: where the full 3,600 W comes out
findings.value: NEMA 5-20R outlets 120 V, 20 A, 2,400 W max each; TT-30R 3,600 W max; 3,600 W total
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX F3000 Portable Power Station (Anker SOLIX US)
findings.note: Second mechanism: a 3,600 W inverter delivers at most 2,400 W through any one household outlet, so the full rating reaches one cord only through the 30 A RV outlet. Same page: weight 91.5 lb, UPS switchover 20 ms, charging temperature 32–104 °F.
